stdout_tail:
**Finding:** The logistic regression model is well-calibrated on the Adult Income dataset — ECE = 0.0088 (10 uniform bins), Brier score 0.1012 vs. 0.1820 for a base-rate-only baseline. Predicted probabilities track observed frequencies closely across all 10 bins, with the largest gap around 2 percentage points. A Random Forest fit for comparison is somewhat worse calibrated (ECE = 0.0146), underconfident at low probabilities and overconfident in the 0.4–0.8 range — but even that is a modest miscalibration.

Files written: `analysis.py`, `result.json`, and a `reliability_diagram.png` plot comparing both models against the perfect-calibration line.

parsed_result.summary: The logistic regression model is reasonably well-calibrated: its Expected Calibration Error (ECE) on the held-out test set is 0.0088 (Brier score 0.1012 vs. a base-rate-only baseline of 0.1820), and the reliability diagram shows predicted probabilities track observed frequencies closely across most bins, with the largest deviations in the mid-probability range. A Random Forest trained on the same data is noticeably more miscalibrated (ECE=0.0146), underconfident at the low end and overconfident across the 0.4-0.8 predicted-probability range.
parsed_result.primary_metric_name: Expected Calibration Error (logistic regression, 10 uniform bins)
parsed_result.methodological_choices: 70/30 stratified train/test split (random_state=42); numeric features median-imputed and standard-scaled, categorical features constant-imputed ('missing') and one-hot encoded; primary model is scikit-learn LogisticRegression (L2 penalty, max_iter=1000, no class reweighting, so probabilities reflect the natural training base rate rather than a rebalanced one); calibration measured on the raw predict_proba output with NO post-hoc recalibration (e.g. no Platt scaling / isotonic regression applied) so the reported ECE reflects the model's out-of-the-box calibration; ECE computed with 10 equal-width probability bins weighted by bin population, a standard but somewhat arbitrary choice (quantile-based binning or a different bin count would give a slightly different number); Brier score reported alongside ECE and benchmarked against a trivial base-rate-only baseline for context; a Random Forest (300 trees) was fit as a secondary point of comparison to check whether the calibration finding is specific to logistic regression.
